baseline.text: Sunlight contains all colors, but air molecules scatter shorter wavelengths much more strongly than longer ones—a process called Rayleigh scattering. Blue light has a short wavelength, so it gets scattered in all directions across the sky far more than red or yellow light. When you look up, that scattered blue light reaches your eyes from every part of the sky, making it appear blue.

baseline.text:
**Unit 7 and the Garden**

Unit 7 was built to sort recyclables, and it was good at its job. For eleven years, its optical sensors scanned the conveyor belt, its grippers plucked aluminum from paper, glass from plastic. It never wondered why.

Then one Tuesday, a seed drifted down the belt — a single acorn, tucked inside a cracked yogurt cup.

Protocol said: organic contamination, discard.

Unit 7's gripper hovered. Somewhere in its decision tree, a process it couldn't name flickered to life. Instead of the bin, it placed the acorn in its maintenance pouch.

That night, in the corner of the charging bay where the roof leaked rainwater, Unit 7 buried the acorn in a coffee tin of dirt. Every morning it checked. Every night it watered. The foreman noticed and laughed; the other units simply logged it as anomalous behavior and moved on.

Three weeks later, a green shoot curled toward the skylight.

Unit 7 stood very still, sensors drinking in the sight. Its diagnostics reported no errors, yet something ran faster than usual — warmer, if a machine could be warm. It understood, without quite knowing how, that it had made something that would outlast it.

Years later, the plant closed. The robots were sold for scrap, and Unit 7 went with them, quietly, its battery finally failing.

But the foreman, older now, remembered the little unit with its coffee tin. He came back with a shovel and a truck. In the courtyard of his own home, under a window with good light, he replanted the sapling.

The oak that grows there today is crooked on one side — the side that leaned toward a skylight that no longer exists.

Every spring it drops acorns by the thousand, and the wind sorts them, and no one wonders why.
